How dare you accuse me of being a friendless loser! I have loads of friends! Their names are R2-D2 and Clippy and Arnold and Rosie the Maid. They all live in my rucksack, ready and waiting should I need somebody to dupe a security guard or fill the air around me with explosive chaff. All except Clippy, that is. He's too chonky to stuff in a bag, which can make for tricky mission extractions, but he compensates for that with his generous selection of *voice drops six octaves* FULLY LOADED AUTOCANNONS.

According to recent reports, with friends like these, who needs human allies? It's time to play stealth tactics sim Cyber Knights: Flashpoint the way it was meant to be played: skulking in a hole while buzzing, clanking mechabastards cleanse the map of any and all defenders. Don't spare the lead, Rosie. You were not built to understand mercy.

Let's try that again: wireheady heist-me-do Cyber Knights: Flashpoint has received a major enhancement adding a fresh player class, the Drone Pilot, billed by developers Trese Brothers as "the most complex" and among the most "flexible" of the game's Neuromantic vocations. The Drone Pilot arrives alongside a new pet system they'll be using down the road for "warhunds and assassin cats". Right now, though, the only "pets" at your disposal appear to be those drones. Here's what they're good for: "jamming enemy systems, disabling security devices in passing, hijacking enemy drones to turn on their own side, or trailing fields of shredding nano-chaff and squad-boosting support zones wherever the drone flies.".

In a recent development, drones come in three types, light (fast and best for stealthy support), medium (a mix of support and combat-oriented), and heavy (flying forts and/or stomping murder mechs). Light or medium drones are deployed from your backpack, and auto-extract when you do, no matter where they are. Heavy drones deploy alongside you at mission start, and have to be within nine metres of you when you extract, potentially trapping you on the map. Each drone chassis has its own weapon and armour setup, plus a choice of modules that grant Talents (abilities).

Sources indicate that while rolling a Drone Pilot might seem like an opportunity to forgo any and all squidgy organic accomplices, the substantial catch is that Drone Pilots and their mecha mates share action and movement points. While using the Full Pilot talent, you can transfer AP to a drone so that it can move and fight like a full separate character. While using the Auto-Pilot talent, you'll only share bonus MP. There's also the option to multi-class, with Trese Brothers noting that "dipping into another class can significantly increase their flexibility or buff their personal abilities with just a few talents from an alternate tree".

In a recent development, as for how you'll get your hands on the Drone Pilot class, their costs make them a poor fit for teams with a power level below three, so they aren't among the New Game options. You'll be able to recruit them in the Underworld Hub and also, turn characters into drone pilots once you acquire a Pilot Wire cybernetic implant and the requisite cyber surgery. The Pilot Wire uses up a Deep Brain slot, making the class incompatible with the Hacker or Wireghost classes. Beyond that, you can reach out to a smuggler or broker to get access to new and better drones and pilot cybernetics.

In a recent development, pettable killdroids aside, Trese Brothers are continuing work on Cyber Knight's mod support. The latest upgrade adds features for official language translation mods and Attribute bonus tweaking, alongside expanded Legwork options. They're also labouring away on a modkit preview project of some kind. Read more on Steam.

Industry observers note that new to Cyber Knights? Congratulations on digesting all the above gibberish about weaponised WALL-Es. I can only assume you read the whole thing in hopes of further talk of "assassin cats", but alas, Trese Brothers are maintaining an ominous silence. Instead, here is what Nic Reuben (RPS in peace) had to say about the game in our 2025 review: "Don't let its initial cyber-posturing and sheer amount of systems intimidate you. Cyber Knights: Flashpoint is wider than it is oppressively deep, while still being rich enough to offer up some excellently tense and entertaining stealth tactics.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that despite being set in the past, WoW: Forever is an attempt to capture the spirit of the old game by injecting it with new quirks that challenge new and returning players alike to approach it differently than any other version of the MMO.
  • Blizzard has remarked that its goal is to "unsolve" the game as best it can so players don't settle into the same routines they're used to.
  • It's a lofty goal that can't be achieved without persistently fiddling with the knobs that encourage players to do one thing over another—which is the very thing that differentiates WoW: Forever from WoW Classic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that despite being set in the past, WoW: Forever is an attempt to capture the spirit of the old game by injecting it with new quirks that challenge new and returning players alike to approach it differently than any other version of the MMO. This is why familiar old dungeons can drop new loot, like an armor set that turns you into a snake.

Blizzard has remarked that its goal is to "unsolve" the game as best it can so players don't settle into the same routines they're used to. This is especially true for min-maxed strategies that threaten to suck the fun out of enjoying the game, or "the journey", as Blizzard likes to call it.

It's a lofty goal that can't be achieved without persistently fiddling with the knobs that encourage players to do one thing over another—which is the very thing that differentiates WoW: Forever from WoW Classic.

This week, Blizzard stepped in to fix a problem that was brewing in its 40-player MOBA-esque PvP mode Alterac Valley. Players were avoiding PvP altogether, turning it into a glorified reputation farm.

"We’ve seen that players in Alterac Valley were frequently completing the battleground without capturing the objectives, so we’ve made some adjustments to incentivize a focus on the objectives rather than rushing to kill the enemy faction’s general," community manager Kaivax wrote.

The patch basically broke a popular 'zerg' strategy where one side rushed to end the match as fast as possible by beefing up the NPC defenders that stood in their way. Blizzard shifted some of the reputation and honor you'd normally get from killing the generals to the other objectives so players are encouraged to engage with the whole mode.

According to recent reports, but, as I've seen with changes like this in the past few weeks, many players are upset that they can't just spam it for the rewards, and that others have already reaped the benefits of the old strategy. There are people in Reddit threads doing the math to highlight how much efficiency has been lost (it doesn't seem like much) and questioning the point of doing Alterac Valley at all.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

While I sympathize with not wanting to do something that feels like a chore, it's a far worse problem to have an entire part of the game flattened into an AFK farm. Alterac Valley is supposed to feel like a large-scale war where you look at a substantial map and choose what objectives are worth fighting over as you try to weaken the enemy forces. The loot you get from maxing out your reputation with the associated factions is meant to be a reward for putting in the effort to learn what it takes to win.

The whole pitch for WoW: Forever is that it's not going to ditch everything with a upcoming expansion every few years. Numbers can be tweaked down the line if the reputation grind is too much of a slog, but the mode should be fun to play so it's not treated like a box to check off in your character's journey. An inert PvP mode ruins the spirit of the MMO far more than a slightly longer reputation grind does.

Industry observers note that I think this is a good example of a healthy change that demonstrates Blizzard is committed to protecting core parts of the experience from becoming a treadmill that nobody enjoys. WoW: Forever's strengths are the ways it encourages you to participate in systems that aren't there to fill progression bars. As Harvey said in his WoW: Forever review, "Forever is proof that old-school MMO design deserves a second chance," and that requires taking a stance on what the game is and isn't meant to be.

In a recent development, in an unexpected move, Blizzard announced it's keeping some of the nostalgia-laiden content from the previous season, Season of Hell's Legacy, as a permanent addition. This is unusual, as the ephemeral nature of live seasons means new content goes away at the end of each season.

Season of Hell's Legacy paid tribute to Diablo's legacy and its 30th anniversary by introducing a lot of content inspired by previous Diablo games, chiefly Diablo 2. The list includes the return of iconic character Deckard Cain, a recreation of Old Tristram, and a substantial fight against the three Prime Evils - Diablo, Baal, and Mephisto - in their classic forms.

Sources indicate that "We heard overwhelming requests for features from Season of Hell's Legacy to carry forward as permanent game features," Blizzard wrote in Season 16's announcement post. "While the entire season couldn't come along for the ride, we are implementing the following features with the launch of Season of Tyrael's Gambit that will carry forward in both Eternal and Seasonal realms.".

So here's what's sticking around:.

Season of Tyrael's Gambit kicks off 1st December, so you still have time to access all of that in Diablo 4 until Season 15 ends. Certain things, such as craftable items, won't return, so you may as well try them while you can. That said, Blizzard is aware of the love some of those items have, and the developer said it may bring them back in the future.

  • Fatshark's co-op rat-whacker Warhammer: Vermintide 2 is getting some new mod tools.
  • According to recent reports, "While the Vermintide 2 Software Development Kit and the Vermintide Modding Framework have been out for years, these mostly only facilitated the development of purely code-related mods," the devs write on the official site.
  • "The Mod Tools is a public release of our internal Stingray developer tools for Vermintide 2!" they continue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pick up your feet, mayflies! Fatshark's co-op rat-whacker Warhammer: Vermintide 2 is getting some new mod tools. It already has a public SDK and modding framework, you say? Ah, but the new mod tools are better. They are a public-facing incarnation of the very same digital spellcraft Fatshark use to create the official levels and characters.

According to recent reports, "While the Vermintide 2 Software Development Kit and the Vermintide Modding Framework have been out for years, these mostly only facilitated the development of purely code-related mods," the devs write on the official site. "There was no support for any other type of mod, and so creating mods that involved creating upcoming assets has been either extremely difficult or impossible. But no more!

"The Mod Tools is a public release of our internal Stingray developer tools for Vermintide 2!" they continue. "This powerful set of tools will allow modders to work their magic on both editing and creating anything from custom levels, models, textures, particles, animations, and more! While it will probably take them a little while to cook exciting new mods, this marks a new era for Vermintide 2 modded content!".

Sources indicate that OK, that's enough exclamation marks. The latest mod tools are available to all owners of the game. You'll be able to find them in your Steam library, listed as "Modding Tools" and "Modding Tools content".

Fatshark have had to make a few "compromises" to get the upcoming mod toolkit finished. "The weapon pack and the level that we mentioned in the past has been put on hold," the devs write. "We still want to get back to that, especially the weapon pack, but for now there is no active development on that. It’s crucial for us that we have transparency here, and while we are not working on these things, we do stick with our games! We have plans both near and far for Vermintide 2.".

The Mod Tools rollout accompanies a change in server support. Hitherto, the Vermintide 2 modding scene has been split between the game's "Official Realm", where only officially sanctioned mods are allowed - "typically reserved for QoL mods that did not affect the experience much", the devs say – and the howling Chaos Wastes of the Modded Realm, which lets you install whatever grievous warpstone chicanery you please, at the cost of having no progression.

The lack of progression in Modded Realm has resulted in these servers "not seeing much use outside of niche communities", Fatshark claim. They're addressing that by, as you may guess, adding a Modded-only offline progression system, allowing players to scoop up loot and XP while performing weird experiments on the simulation.

According to recent reports, fatshark say they no longer have the capacity to keep up with mod approvals in the Official Realm, to say nothing of problems resulting from mods that have stopped receiving updates. They don't seem to have a solution for this, yet. They do, however, have a solution for an on-going lack of players in the dedicated Versus servers: shut down those servers! Let them crumple to dust!

"Versus is still playable, but it will be through community hosted games found through the Custom Game or the Lobby Browser," the devs assure. "This is already how most games of Versus are played, so we don’t think it will be a huge shake up in any shape or form, and it puts more of a focus on the Custom Game format where players have more control over the ruleset.".

According to recent reports, the shutdown will happen alongside the game's next update – Gifts of the Wolf Father, due in early December, which will rework the game's talent balance, update the weapon icons, and make the glow of different runes easier to distinguish from afar. Look out for more details down the line. In the meantime, please thrill my pointy ears with talk of Vermintide 2 mods. I've never touched that side of the game, and am wondering if there are any Skaven megaprojects I'm missing out on.

According to recent reports, things continue to get messy in the community of players working on getting Grand Theft Auto 6 working on PC. The previous frontrunner, Project Leonida, got their Discord server and GitHub repository taken down by Rockstar, but others have seemingly stepped in to finish the job.

Industry observers note that the most up-to-date build of GTA 6 was allegedly leaked earlier this week by notorious leaker CyberLeek. This is a supposedly near-final build of the game's Xbox version, and it's seemingly being used as the basis for the recent work to port the game to PC.

Unsurprisingly, most of these communities of modders rely almost exclusively on generative-AI tools like Claude and Antigravity to decompile and recompile the console version of GTA 6. That has always been the case, but the CyberLeek build only invited even more to ask AI chatbots to make the PC port for them.

X user chasm has been following developments in the GTA 6 decompile and recompile communities, and recently shared some of the prompts the so-called vibe-coders are using - a few of whom livestreamed the process.

"Make no mistakes," one modder prompted the AI chatbot. "Keep finding more stuff and working and pushing," another eloquently asked. "Work faster," asked another. "There has to be a faster way to iterate than this," they continued.

As for how far some of the remaining communities have managed to get, this video allegedly reveals the game running on PC. This goes beyond the boot-up screen, which modders were able to reach within hours of CyberLeek's build alleged leaking.

It has been revealed that the footage runs at sub-5fps, but the visuals look to have rendered normally. Assuming Rockstar doesn't also shut down the modders who remain active, we may see another progress enhancement.

If you're already playing Rockstar's latest on consoles, the Eurogamer GTA 6 walkthrough offers comprehensive guides on relationship mechanics, how the latest Criminal Profile system works, a list of all safe codes and more.

#167497. Tech Report: This Emerging Artist Is a Hit Restaurateur

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2205 w)

Tech Report: This Emerging Artist Is a Hit Restaurateur

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before.
  • It has been revealed that on one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades.
  • Recent findings suggest that the twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Borgo sits on one of those blocks in the high 20s that you swear you’ve never been down before. The restaurant opened in 2024 but feels like it’s been there forever, a place with a natural hum and not an ounce of perspiration. Its clientele is specific but unpredictable; when I went there this summer for lunch with a movie producer, we spotted a powerful name-brand media executive, an architectural bigwig who designs the homes of billionaires, and a two-time Academy Award–winning actor. A few nights later, I sat near Walter Isaacson, who’s a regular. And don’t just take it from Elon Musk’s biographer. Matthew Schneier, the chief restaurant critic at Latest York magazine, recently named Borgo the city’s best all-around restaurant.

It has been revealed that on one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades. He met Ross Bleckner there, and David Salle. He used to have a massive loft studio in Williamsburg, but as rents went up, he moved deeper into Brooklyn, to Fort Greene, where he built a studio in his basement.

Recent findings suggest that the twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art. That’s because he was Andrew Tarlow—the painter and restaurateur who kick-started the Brooklyn aesthetic with his restaurant Diner and, yes, also owns Borgo.

After launching that instant hit in an old, reclaimed diner, Tarlow opened five more era-defining Brooklyn spots before finally venturing into Manhattan with Borgo. All along, he’s still been the artist who got a job at The Odeon so that he could meet his heroes. He’s still painting away in his brownstone, doodling on notepads during concept meetings. He’s had indicates recently at galleries such as Tiwa Select; he’s loosely associated with the Galerie Sardine extended universe; and he’s someone whose work I’ve been told about for years by those in the know.

As they put it, Tarlow is an emerging artist who happens to own the best all-around restaurant in Manhattan, as well as a bunch of other successful spots in Brooklyn.

In a recent development, “I realized, opening Borgo, that I really loved working in restaurants—and not that I had forgotten, but I hadn’t actually worked services in a while until I opened,” Tarlow told me during a studio visit. “And then, in a similar way, I think—I love making paintings. I actually will paint forever, no matter what happens.”.

The studio had dozens of unstretched canvases heaped on the ground, some still rolled up, and others hanging via a pin on the studio wall. They showed figures grappling with pain in fierce color-blocked fields, automatic-painting abstractions, faces fading into other faces. One painting was a portrait of the artist Joe Bradley, a friend.

According to recent reports, the studio is in the basement of the Fort Greene brownstone where Tarlow has lived for two decades with his wife, Kate Huling, raising four kids in a kind of neo-boho paradise. There were no studio assistants, no art handlers, no frames, no boxes, no packaging—just the artist and the work.

“It was kind of just as chaotic as everything else there, but in the most perfect warm embrace of a way. I saw the pure energy that he put into his paintings and the stories that they told,” claims Alex Tieghi-Walker, the founder of Tiwa Select, calling from London. “So many artists could be quite—rightfully so, but quite precious with their works. And I love that Andrew was just like, ‘Oh, pull out the ones you’re taking and just take them in an Uber home.’”.

Tarlow grabbed at a canvas bare-handed, one with a bit of a conceptual bent, and put it up on an easel.

It has been revealed that “I’ve had this up on the wall for a while now, and I just continued to look at it because I’m happy with it. I’m also a little unsettled—I mean, I’m showing you the inside of my drawers. I’m also a little unsettled by how far it’s gone abstract-wise.”.

He told me he couldn’t really do his other job, the restaurant job, without painting at odd hours. They’re totally separate, but complementary in a cosmic way.

Sources indicate that “What are the processes? Like you said, for some people, it’s nine to five. Then you listen to the news, smoke a cigarette, drink coffee. It’s either working or it’s not. The door either opens or it’s not,” Tarlow said, gesturing around to his studio. “But I’m going to go here every day, and I’m going to push some paint on canvas.”.

It has been revealed that diner opened in 1999, a few years after Tarlow moved to the desolate southern tip of Broadway in Williamsburg—where the crumbling street dead-ends into the East River. While looking for a cheap studio space, he found a 6,000-square-foot loft across the street from an abandoned diner from the 1920s. The loft’s landlord bought the diner, and in 1999, Tarlow opened Diner with then partner Mark Firth—and watched as it was patronized by only the artists across the street.

“You could stand outside the restaurant in those days and not see a single person walk by,” he told Bon Appetit in 2010.

Tarlow kept expanding. He opened Marlow & Sons, and then the butcher shop and specialty food store Marlow & Daughters. He founded a bakery, She Wolf, and a literary magazine, Diner Journal. He operated the restaurant at the Wythe Hotel, but only for a few years. Instead of doing the easy thing, Vegas-ifying Diner in some newly introduced development on the Williamsburg waterfront, he got even weirder, opening a nautical bar called Achilles Heel in a far-out corner of Greenpoint.

A dealer with a gallery in Tribeca was the first, but far from the last, to tell me I had to check out Tarlow’s paintings. After an introduction was brokered, Tarlow invited me to lunch at Borgo this past summer. The restaurant has many fantastic pork-laden dishes, but we ate almost entirely vegetables, as well as one very elegant, simple piece of fish. A summer lunch. We fell into an easy patter, talking about exhibitions, other artists—but mostly his painting practice. He’d been working on Long Island, not on the East End but in the middle. He’d had a few shows. There was discussion of representation. He spoke about all this with an unpracticed earnestness and complete confidence. He sounded like a very prominent emerging artist, which, at 56, he is.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t know if it’s just age or time, or I was too much of a young person, or a young mind, but I’ve been more secure with my ability to hold all these things in the same time,” he told me back in the studio. “I can go work tonight in the restaurant and feel perfectly confident in that work, and I can show you this work and feel perfectly confident in this work. Whereas, I think, as a young person, I felt like, Am I fake?”.

According to recent reports, sometimes it’s not the enfant terrible who breaks out—it’s the working parent, the person with a desk job, the successful entrepreneur who back-ends into revolutionary art making. Think William Carlos Williams writing “The Red Wheelbarrow” while working as a doctor in Rutherford, New Jersey. Or Ruth Asawa making art in her kitchen while raising six children in San Francisco. Or Jeff Koons working on Wall Street in order to earn money to make his sculptures. Having a demanding job actually granted them the freedom to be artists. Tarlow started drawing during restaurant concept meetings.

Industry observers note that sometimes Tarlow hangs his own paintings upstairs in his brownstone’s salon room, or at his house on Long Island, to see what they look like in the wild. The paintings have a confident thrust to them, with the colors bold-blocked in a way that reminds me of Albert Oehlen, drawing from Roman and Greek mythology in Twombly-esque riffs: visages multiplying and fading like a Kippenberger-ian pomo ride into the ether. Sure, any painter who’s spent time in Europe since the 1990s has wanted to be Martin Kippenberger. But Tarlow has an actual connection to him: Like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a lover of Italian food and good wine, and he made art to hang in restaurants. And like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a restaurant owner, balancing his studio practice with running Capri, a Venice, California, spot in which he invested after moving to Los Angeles in 1989. According to those present at the time, Kippenberger became a part-owner of the place because, as the artist put it, “You can’t get a decent Bolognese in Los Angeles.”.

Recent findings suggest that as a bartender at The Odeon, Tarlow maintained a working painting studio but found it hard to produce art. After opening Diner, he skipped painting sessions in favor of opening businesses and starting a family. Once that duality settled, he started drawing on the move, carrying sketchbooks and working through potential paintings. Eventually, once the kids got old enough, he built out a studio in a nook of his 19th-century basement.

According to recent reports, “I really started painting back downstairs. Let’s just say, after dinner, it was 8 p.m. and they were watching Nemo. No one actually needs me, they’re totally happy. My wife’s up there, everyone’s laughing, giggling with little fish,” he stated. “And I can just walk down here and do my thing. Having it in my house for sure is the only way I could do this amount of work, and for sure even get to this place. Because I do think you have to do a certain amount of work to get to this place unless you’re just a born prodigy. But when you think about the genius of Picasso or whomever, he made a million fucking paintings.”.

Tarlow didn’t really show anyone his work for a long time.

“I met Andrew socially. I knew his restaurants way before I knew Andrew. And one day he was like, ‘Come and see my studio,’” Tieghi-Walker tells me. “It did not surprise me at all that he had an art studio in his basement and that these were the types of works he was creating.”.

In a recent development, the show at Tiwa Select was on view right as Tarlow was getting ready to open Borgo. There was a certain amount of unconscious transference, Tarlow told me. For the Tiwa dinner, instead of creating name placards, the artist hand-sketched an artwork of each guest’s name on the paper tablecloth. Now, when a regular makes a reservation at Borgo, Tarlow will elegantly sketch out their name on the paper tablecloth.

Sources indicate that the showcasing of his art at Borgo marks the first time Tarlow has put his own work on the premises of his own restaurant. Tarlow doesn’t exactly promote this. When I asked about it, he told me that only one of his own works was up at the moment, then changed the subject. Alex Levy, the media strategist and theater producer, has been a regular at Borgo since it opened. “Borgo is the grown-up Platonic ideal of what a restaurant can be,” he stated. After several visits, Levy, who also collects a bit of contemporary art, noticed what was on the walls.

According to recent reports, “I complimented one of the paintings, and Andrew noted, ‘It’s by my daughter.’ And then he pointed to another one and said, ‘That’s by me,’” Levy claims. “I had no idea that there’s this whole other part of him.”.

It has been revealed that like Tarlow, Levy balances two seemingly divergent but strangely complementary careers—as a speechwriter on one hand, a Tony Award winner on the other—and Tarlow invited him to see his studio on Long Island. Levy bought a painting immediately. Seeing the studio, Levy notes, helped him realize, to some extent, what the special sauce is behind a place like Borgo. It’s for incredibly confident, hyperproductive creative types, run by an artist who has complete faith in his ability to work.

And for Tarlow, the focus and passion in one arena lead right into the passion for the other.

It has been revealed that “I’m also being very present for your needs in the same way as I’m trying to be very present with these paintings,” he noted. “They’re not separate boats. When the restaurant’s working, I feel creative inside of it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, at this point on Marshals, I never use Cal’s full name, Pete Calvin. His nickname is used far more than his full name, and now, Cal’s putting in the work to make sure his team has nicknames like him. For example, as Season 2 of Marshals has been airing on the 2026 TV schedule, I’ve noticed Cal calling Kayce Coyote a lot. So, with all this in mind, I asked Logan Marshall-Green, who plays Cal, what’s up with the nicknames, and specifically Kayce’s.

Back when Yellowstone was on, there was a lot of drama involving wolves and Kayce. So, I was a bit surprised when Cal started calling him Coyote (pronounced “ky-oat” instead of “ky-oh-tee”). However, it felt fitting for the Dutton family member. When I asked Marshall-Green about it, he told me it was an important thing that he and Luke Grimes wanted Cal to use with Kayce, too, and it all ties back to their military history:.

That was something Luke and I both were talking about being SEALs. You don't call people by their first names; you just don't. And so, also with the team, it's been key to try to find nicknames. So Luke was very adamant about finding a nickname for him that I could use. That was something that [creator Spencer Hudnut] came up with. I think it's like kind of a play on Coyote. I'm not sure if I gave him that name or if somebody else gave him Coyote and we just started calling him Coyote because of other people.

In a recent development, so, the backstory behind the nickname is unknown, at least to Logan Marshall-Green. However, it is something that’s important to Cal and Kayce’s shared history. If I had to guess, Kayce got the nickname while they were both SEALs, and it’s just stuck. I personally hope Cal is the one responsible for it, and maybe someday that can be addressed in the show.

It has been revealed that while we wait for that backstory, Marshall-Green is putting in the work to get the rest of his team nicknames. In the show, we’ve heard Ash Santos’ Andrea referred to as Dre on multiple occasions, and that was a creation of the Cal actor. He personally went to Santos and Spencer Hudnut to ask them about it. He’s also trying to get nicknames for Tatanka Means’ Miles and Arielle Kebbel’s Belle to stick. Explaining all of that, he said:.

But you know, like Dre is something I approached Spencer and Ash about because I thought that would be a perfect name for Cal to call [her], because that's who he hired first for the team. And we're still trying to work – you know, there's Dust Cloud for Miles’, for Tatanka’s character. And I came up with a really good – I thought it was a really good nickname for Belle, but Ariel didn't love it. So yeah.

According to recent reports, so, we have Dre and Coyote. We have Dust Cloud too. However, Belle still does not have a nickname because it sounds like Kebbel vetoed it. Knowing Cal and Belle’s relationship, that feels hilariously fitting. However, I do hope that someday she can get a nickname too.

Now, to see this team (and their nicknames) in action, you can catch upcoming episodes of Marshals on CBS every Sunday. You can also stream them the day after with a Paramount+ subscription.

Gemini's Newly introduced AI Agent Is Surprisingly Useful (If You Use Google for Everything)

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that google loves a rebrand.
  • To use Task, open Gemini and create a newly introduced chat.
  • Of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that google loves a rebrand. What started off as "Spark" is now "Task" in Gemini—not to be confused with Google Tasks, the to-do app. Google took its Spark AI agent, which used to live in a separate tab, and integrated it into the Gemini interface. Gemini Task is available globally, and it’s completely free to use for some. That said, some features are limited to the U.S. and, of course, subject to some pretty strict usage limits. While not exactly a replacement for ChatGPT Dots or Meta Muse, you can think of Gemini Task as a controlled version of an AI agent that can do quite a lot in the background.

To use Task, open Gemini and create a newly introduced chat. You’ll see a Task tab next to Chat. Switch to it, and start writing your prompt. (You’ll also see some suggested options here.) Type your task or action and press "Send." The feature works best if you’ve already enabled Personal Intelligence on your Google account, and have connected services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos as well. You can then tag “@Gmail” to use your Gmail account, or even a third-party connector. Task natively supports automation, so you can say something like, "run this task once every day," and the AI will add it to your Scheduled Tasks section.

Of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks. And, in my experience, it works really well. It reminded me of this article's due date, that I have a couple of pitches in my inbox to review, that a credit card bill is due soon, and that there are some holidays around the corner.

Gemini is very good at retrieving information from emails and taking action. For example, I created an automation that collects all my coffee orders for the month and presents the data in Google Sheets. I then asked Task to create a subscription manager for me. Instead of paying for a third-party app, it took a few minutes to collate the services I pay for into one list. It even accounted for the currency differences (some subscriptions are in USD, some in INR) and gave me a tally in INR, along with things like average monthly cost, and more.

It has been revealed that while Gemini can connect to the open web, it's quite a hostile place right now for an AI bot. Websites are blocking agents from accessing their pages, which hinders their effectiveness. I asked Gemini to create a task that monitors the price of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones daily. For this, it asked my permission to spin up a remote browser, and loaded up Amazon, only to be blocked instantly. It did succeed in opening Croma though (a national retailer in India), but it took almost a minute for it to figure out that the price had not dropped below what I asked for. Would it be quicker and less resource-intensive if I did this myself? Yes, but the fact that Gemini can do this every evening like clockwork is the real advantage—as long as the websites comply, that is.

Recent findings suggest that if you're going to try Task in Gemini for free, there are some limitations you should know about. The free proposal only lets you run tasks once per day, and you can’t be granular about the exact timing. (Paid Gemini looks have no such restrictions.) You can only run 10 tasks at the same time, while the limit is 50 tasks for AI Pro owners. Compute-based usage limits will also apply, based on your plan. The free access is currently live in India, the U.S., Canada, Australia, Japan, and South Korea.

In a recent development, some features, though, are only for U.S. customers. Gemini’s feature that lets you call businesses on your behalf is restricted to the States, as is the ability to forward emails to [email protected] to automatically turn the contents of the email into a task (like adding a college schedule to your calendar). U.S. users can also connect their Google Wallet account to set up payments at supported stores.

Industry observers note that gemini Task is not a proactive agent, nor is it trying to be. You still have to check the work. You have to approve any important steps, and if a website blocks AI models, there’s not a lot Gemini can do about it. For someone like me, who’s all-in on the Google ecosystem, I do see value in Gemini Task. The deep and robust Gmail integration is worth it alone. If you’re on the free blueprint, set up a couple of background tasks related to Gmail, Google Drive, or background research that run every morning, and call it a day. And if you’re paying for AI Pro, you can get a lot more done.

Hollow Knight: Silksong developer Team Cherry has announced it will host a 'Cherry Time Special Presentation' on 27th November, bringing more information to light about the game's first substantial DLC offering, Sea of Sorrows. We know that the free update will be nautically-themed - hence the eponymous 'sea' - and will feature latest bosses, areas and so on, but other than that, information about what's coming is vague.

But it seems that's not all; as well as more information about the mysterious upgrade to the hit Metroidvania game, the studio has also announced "a bunch" of other "exciting announcements." Curious.

The Cherry Time Special Presentation will kick off at 7am PT / 10am ET / 3pm GMT / 4pm CEST. I'll embed the video below, so check back here at the time if you need a bookmark.

Recently, and more than a year after its initial release, physical versions of Hollow Knight: Silksong finally began arriving on players' doorsteps. Whilst these editions contained mostly expected information, there was an unforeseen mention of "free content packs" that would be arriving alongside the Sea of Sorrow DLC. Will we hear more about these as part of this new showcase? We don't have too long to find out.

It seems likely, though. "The world of Hollow Knight: Silksong will expand with free content packs," the booklet read in the physical editions. "Prepare for even more adventures filled with latest friends, new abilities, and new ferocious foes!" Team Cherry has repeatedly confirmed plans for post-launch Silksong support, but other than this upcoming DLC, we don't really know what that entails.

It has been revealed that additionally, Sea of Sorrow's original release window was a vague 2026 - will we see it shadowdrop as part of this stream? Stranger things have happened, especially in the world of Hollow Knight….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Glagstone's "1-bit" aesthetic is a homage to Macintosh games of the late 1980s, cut with elements of art deco, Expressionism and film noir, but it looks like that mainly because it began life on lo-fi indie handheld Playdate.

According to recent reports, in transplanting this eerie, story-driven city-builder to Steam, developers Valerii Krasnoselskii and Evgenii Kirichenko have fleshed out the tasty throwback art and shored up connections between the game's management and story layers, while leaving the crux of the experience untouched: you are the newly appointed governor of a remote northern island, contested by rival nations. You have come here to harvest the island's rich mineral resources, and now, the island is trying to drive you nuts.

You start by building homes and roads, getting fish to the warehouse, and churning out coal for the Crown. You'll also need to get the local lighthouse operational, so that you can see the city you're maintaining amid recurring fog, storms and darkness.

According to the devs, who've written a longer account of their project for 80.lv, it's supposed to feel like a simple sandbox, at first. But it has a creeping undertow. Visiting ships bring both opportunity and peril – admitting them to port is a gamble. The coastline is worryingly indefinite, in ways that can't quite be attributed to the tides. The locals are secretive, demanding and a little sinister. They talk of strange masked rituals, Silver Ladies, Shed Skins, and coves where you don't go during an eclipse. The Crown's orders, meanwhile, make less and less sense, and the waves keep coughing up peculiar objects. Sometimes, you could swear you hear singing through the surf.

A lot of the associated Dreadful Lore appears to arrive in the form of notebook marginalia, item descriptions, and sailor anecdotes that need to be coaxed forth with the promise of liquor. There are also pop-up events that may shape the morale and loyalty of your townsfolk. Those masked festivals, for example: they'll cost you production, but the glint in the village elder's eye suggests that refusing to give people time off for the Old Listening might be… reckless.

Sources indicate that it all feels like an elaborate port fable from Failbetter's Sunless Sea. Or a standalone episode from fellow "1-bit" coastal sojourn World of Horror. You probably don't need me to tell you that Poe and Lovecraft are among the explicit influences. The developers – who are based in Belgrade and Basel - have also taken inspiration from the Svalbard and Novaya Zemlya archipelagoes. I've just googled Svalbard. It has very pretty reindeer. Haven't dug up any reports of kraken and mermaids just yet, but I'm sure they're out there.

Glagstone is coming to PC next year. Catch it on Steam - they're accepting playtest requests. Speaking as a fan of impenetrable marine murk, I think this looks wonderful. The 80.lv piece is worth reading through, however self-promotional - it includes some savoury titbits on how they've modelled the play of radiance between lighthouse beam and roadside lantern. Did you try the Playdate original? Any comments?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Xbox One had a reasonably strong launch lineup that included juggernauts like Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag and Battlefield 4 launching right alongside the hardware in 2013, but it was originally supposed to have some extremely strong RPG representation in Dragon Age: Inquisition. Well, that's what BioWare told EA, anyway.

Talking to Pembridge TV (timestamp), former Dragon Age series lead and longtime BioWare veteran Mark Darrah says the studio straight-up fibbed when it told EA Inquisition would be a launch day title for the Xbox One generation of consoles.

In a recent development, "The pitch for Dragon Age: Inquisition was that it was going to be a launch title for the Xbox 360, so it was basically supposed to come out in 2013," Darrah claims, before realizing he got his generations mixed up and was really thinking of Xbox One. That console, alongside the PS4, introduced in November 2013, while Dragon Age: Inquisition didn't release until about a full year later in November 2014. "It was literally supposed to be a launch title for the Xbox One.".

Industry observers note that presumably, Darrah is using Xbox One as shorthand for the eighth generation of consoles, because Dragon Age: Inquisition released in tandem on PS4 and Xbox One. That means EA was likely under the impression that the game would be a PS4 launch title as well, which of course didn't happen, and according to Darrah, that was never even the real proposal at BioWare.

"To be clear, we were lying," states Darrah. "It was never gonna happen, and we didn't even build around – like, we didn't pretend and make the team work to that date. We just lied.

"To be honest, Dragon Age: Inquisition got made in large part because they were really happy with Dragon Age 2, and the game was supposed to come out in two-and-a-half years, that seems good, and so they basically were on board, and then we moved it a year, and then we moved it six weeks.".

Naturally, EA probably wasn't too happy about BioWare's switcharoo, but I'm guessing it was more than happy to forgive the studio when Dragon Age: Inquisition became BioWare's best-selling single game at 12 million units sold, a massive overperformance from EA's expectations. Tragically, that would mark a high point as well as a turning point for BioWare, with things largely going downhill from there with Mass Effect: Andromeda, Anthem, and finally Dragon Age: The Veilguard being the commercial nail in the coffin for the studio, which was shut down by EA in October.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft-owned developer platform Github stepped in it earlier today when it posted a message on X celebrating the success of AnyPS5, an open source project that aims to let users port PS5 executables to PC, and then linked that success directly to efforts to port Grand Theft Auto 6 to PC. The message was deleted shortly after it was posted, but not before it was widely noticed and called out for being a very bad idea.

"GTA 6 is finally here, sparking one of the biggest weeks in gaming and open source on Github," the message stated (via Kotaku).

Recent findings suggest that "The repo AnyPS5 has passed 58K stars since its August launch, rewriting PS5 executables to run on Windows and Linux. Does changing where games run cross a legal line? Share your take. Happy GTA VImas!".

Lest there be any misunderstanding, a video that accompanied the post made the GTA 6 connection explicit: "The project rewrites a game's executable so Windows and Linux can run it directly. Performance seems to be the main matter for users wanting to run GTA 6, with one contributor telling the project's community to 'lock in and get your agents to help' if they need to.".

And here's the accompanying video from @github's GTA6 tweet https://t.co/crU9cpOWcsNovember 26, 2026.

The question of whether or not this sort of thing crosses a legal line has, predictably, sparked debate among those who think they have a clear understanding of the answer. What caught most by surprise, though, is that Github—which is owned by Microsoft—would put forth the question in the first place, implicitly suggesting that it might not. GTA 6 publisher Take-Two Interactive has been pretty aggressive with its efforts to keep recompiled versions of GTA 6 from landing on PC, and I can't imagine it would too thrilled with Github—which, I must emphasize, is owned by Microsoft—telling the world that it might actually be okay to go ahead and vibe-code it up.

It has been revealed that that point wasn't missed by redditors, one of whom described it as Github "openly taunting Sony and Rockstar." Even the AnyPS5 subreddit seemed baffled: Redditor superkickstart asked, "Do they have AI running their socials? Lol".

Sources indicate that there's also a little bit of irony in the fact that, until earlier this week, the leading effort to get GTA 6 running on PC was based on an Xbox build of the game posted by GTA 6 leaker Cyberleeks. Beyond that, there are also some very obvious questions about how Github (owned by Microsoft) would react to AI-powered ports of, say, other software:.

Keep up to date with the most vital stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Recent findings suggest that the whole thing is weird, really, because it seems like such an obviously bad idea. The only explanation I can come up with is that a social media manager either didn't think about it, didn't understand it (which would be weird in itself for someone doing social media posts for Github), or just had a big ol' brain fart. Whatever the reason, I imagine someone got a good old-fashioned talking-to about it.

I've reached out to Github and Take-Two for comment and will update if I receive a reply.

More fundamentally, Sea of Sorrow does look considerably larger in scope than any of Hollow Knight’s freebie DLCs, which at most – Godhome, basically – added a small handful of latest locations and a smattering of boss challenges. Silksong’s first expansion appears to be showing off multiple new regions, legions of new enemy types, extra traversal mechanics, and that most desired of prizes among soulslike and soulslike-adjacent fans: untold lore.

Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic put BioWare through "sympathy crunch," says studio veteran

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamesradar

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's often a tragic backstory to any great game in which developers were forced to work way beyond their scheduled hours, often late into nights and even on weekends.
  • Industry observers note that john Winski, a former employee of BioWare going all the way back to 1996, reflects on Knights of the Old Republic's development in a recent conversation with Pembridge TV.
  • In a recent development, that's a lot of crunch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's often a tragic backstory to any great game in which developers were forced to work way beyond their scheduled hours, often late into nights and even on weekends. Usually, the perception is that everyone's working their tail off to get a project out the door in time for whatever deadline is set by the publisher, but in the case of BioWare's seminal 2003 RPG Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, a lot of people highlighted up at the studio just because they felt bad for people who actually had stuff to do.

Industry observers note that john Winski, a former employee of BioWare going all the way back to 1996, reflects on Knights of the Old Republic's development in a recent conversation with Pembridge TV. "I think we worked five months of crunch time," he claims. "We started with Tuesdays and Thursdays, we'd work 12-hour days. Then it became five days a week working 12-hour days. Saturdays, I don't know how long we were doing seven days a week, 12-hour days.".

In a recent development, that's a lot of crunch. Without official numbers to go by, it's hard to know how that stacks up against notoriously crunch-heavy development cycles like The Last of Us 2, Red Dead Redemption 2, and Cyberpunk 2077, but if you're doing the math, that equates to 84-hour work weeks, more than double the average in most places. According to Winski, "a lot of times it was sympathy crunch," meaning workers who weren't required to come into the studio were doing so anyway because they felt bad for those dealing with mandated crunch.

"You don't have any work, but a bunch of other people have to be here, so you're gonna be here too. Which wasn't great, but also, if you look back, it's like, 'I am supporting all those people that have work to do," adds Winski. "Why wouldn't I be? And when you're young, you're kind of stupid and going, 'well, let's just do it', and it worked.".

Can't argue with that. I mean, I'll argue all day long against crunch culture, but there's no denying that Knights of the Old Republic was a huge success, becoming an immediate hit and the best-selling Star Wars game of all time when it released. It's also not just one of the best Star Wars games to this day, it's also one of the most beloved RPGs of all time, proving that, unfortunately, great games can come from problematic working environments.

It has been revealed that on the other hand, I'm reminded of comments from earlier this year made by Fallout co-creator Tim Cain, who offered a different perspective on crunch in the games industry. While he said he's "glad things have changed" and called Fallout's development "unsustainable," Cain said the developers working unreasonable hours on Fallout were doing so because "they loved what [they] were doing." I'd like to think the Knights of the Old Republic team felt the same.

BioWare turned down Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic 2 because LucasArts wanted the RPG done in 18 months.

Sotheby’s Sold the World’s Most Expensive Van Gogh for $190 Million

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, it’s True Colors, from Fresh York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

In a recent development, it’s True Colors, from Fresh York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses. Nvidia has lost more than $2 trillion in market cap since early October, but on Thursday, Anthropic’s IPO minted a class of new billionaires. It’s whiplash. As one dazed art dealer mused aloud on Monday night in the elevator at Sotheby’s: “It seems like money’s lost all its value.” Maybe the money, but not the art. Amid a surreal era of wealth creation and artificial intelligence, once-in-a-century oil-on-canvas masterpieces only get more covetable. Two Van Goghs from the same collectors have now sold for $190 million apiece, both in the span of a year.

Recent findings suggest that one thing remains constant: Everybody has to eat dinner. And increasingly, they’re doing it at Borgo, perhaps the best all-around restaurant in Newly introduced York—where the owner is a semisecret acclaimed painter. I talked to Andrew Tarlow about maintaining a practice as a serious, boundary-pushing painter while running a Manhattan restaurant.

Industry observers note that speaking of restaurateurs: Michael Chow opened his first Mr. Chow in London nearly 60 years ago, and the spot is still as good as ever. A few works from Chow’s collection, some made specifically for the restaurant, are on view at Gagosian on Madison Avenue. I recently spent some time with him (and, briefly, Larry Gagosian) going through works by Ed Ruscha, Julian Schnabel, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Andy Warhol, as well as many portraits of Chow himself.

We’ve also got reports from the Baby2Baby Gala in LA, the Ballroom Marfa Gala in Harlem, and a special dinner in Tribeca. And all the gossip from the auctions.

Mentioned in this glitch: William Acquavella, Steve Wynn, Steve Cohen, Patrick Drahi, Charles Stewart, Jackie Wachter, Anthony Haden-Guest, Leonardo DiCaprio, Vittoria Ceretti, Jeff Koons, Frances Outred, Andrew Tarlow, Walter Isaacson, Matthew Schneier, Ross Bleckner, David Salle, Valentina Akerman, Joe Bradley, Kate Huling, Alex Tieghi-Walker, Alex Levy, Albert Oehlen, Ignacio Mattos, Louis Shannon, Victoire Bourgois, Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin, Meredith Darrow, Annie Morris, Michael Chow, Lady Gaga, Jim Dine, and Larry Gagosian.

Van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, including fees, Wednesday night at Sotheby’s Breuer building headquarters on Madison. It’s the most expensive work sold at auction this year, and easily among the top 10 priciest things to ever be publicly auctioned. It’s a bit insane to say this, especially about a single canvas that sold for more than the total value of the art set to be on offer at Art Basel Miami Beach next month, but that price feels a bit like a…disappointment? The on-request estimate for the work was $180 million, and the hammer price fell well short of that, at $165 million. Bidding in the room was thin, and the lot was guaranteed by Sotheby’s. Though it’s unclear where the exact guarantee price landed, it was probably around the estimate.

In a recent development, honestly, it’s a relief to the house and the seller—the family of the Argentinian collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier—that this painting sold at all. A Jewish collector bought the work in 1909 from a Paris gallery. His heirs claimed, just days before the auction, that the work was later sold under duress due to Nazi persecution, entitling them to receive restitution. The parties came together over an eleventh hour deal, terms undisclosed, to allow the sale to go through.

So who bought it? The winning bidder in the room was William Acquavella, the patriarch of one of New York’s great art-dealing families, who has an august gallery on the Upper East Side. It’s unclear for whom he bought it. In the past he’s been known to broker art deals on behalf of former Las Vegas casino tycoon Steve Wynn. In 2013, Acquavella was the winning bidder on a Francis Bacon tryptic for $142 million—that time on behalf of Wynn’s ex-wife, the late Elaine Wynn. (The piece is right now on view at LACMA, where Elaine Wynn was a co-chair of the board.) Steve Wynn has been more of a seller than a buyer recently, so the jury’s still out on whom Acquavella was on the phone with Wednesday.

According to recent reports, the $190 million price tag is an almost exact match for the amount someone else paid for another Van Gogh from the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Reports say that, in 2025, Christie’s conducted a private sale where Le Zouave, a Van Gogh portrait of a soldier, sold for $190 million. While there’s no indication that the most recent buyer was someone connected to the AI gold rush, it’s surely indicative of the times that a Van Gogh has sold for 9 figures right around the moment that the seven cofounders of Anthropic have become worth about $20 billion—and around 600 Anthropic employees have become worth more than $100 million. When reached for comment through a rep, Acquavella didn’t get back to me.

In a recent development, — As I walked into Sotheby’s Monday for the first sales of the week, there were clients going downstairs to get their tables at Marcel, where diners can bid tableside while cocktails are served from a bar cart. Other clients went to a sumptuous overflow room with an open bar and a large spread of Marcel goodies. Those lucky enough to snag seats moseyed up to the sales room, where telecom billionaire Patrick Drahi, the owner of Sotheby’s, was standing in the back, near CEO Charles Stewart.

In a recent development, the 6 p.m. start time meant some collectors were still trickling in when Jackie Wachter snagged a Gerhard Richter work for a hammer price of $5 million. In the back of the room, white-jacketed waiters wheeled around with flutes of Champagne for those standing in the back. The writer Anthony Haden-Guest, a longtime Vanity Fair scribe whose book True Colors gave this column its name, walked in and took a seat in the back. One woman started taking selfies. As the contemporary sale got underway, Leonardo DiCaprio and his girlfriend, Vittoria Ceretti, walked down from the skybox and watched as an Agnes Martin hammered at $9.2 million. DiCaprio, a very serious collector, didn’t appear to be bidding, but no matter; he was still there at Sotheby’s. Auction week had officially begun.

— Over at Christie’s, the house sold a Georgia O’Keeffe that had been on view in an apartment in my neighborhood for more than 60 years. Suffice to say, there aren’t many expensive works of art that get discovered in apartments in the vicinity of Tompkins Square Park. I had to savor the lot’s beautifully poetic provenance, a phrasing that I don’t believe has ever been printed in an auction catalog previously: “Property from an East Village Private Collection.” It sold for $4.9 million.

It has been revealed that — The week’s hottest lot? Maybe a sculpture of a dog by Jeff Koons, Bob-Tail, that was first on view at the artist’s still-controversial “Made in Heaven” show. Estimated to sell for an ambitious high estimate of $3.5 million, it hammered at $9 million, or $9.7 million with fees. Former auction chairman Frances Outred stated the sculpture was consigned by a college friend of his who bought it from Anthony d’Offay for a five-figure sum in 1995, “when the art market was in the doldrums and the Jeff Koons market was at its nadir.”.

Recent findings suggest that — For a dinner on Tuesday, Galerie Sardine installed a long table where every seat had a great view of one of the Joe Bradley paintings that had been installed in a space on 9 White Street. It wasn’t exactly a tough sell to get the works at the dinner—Bradley is married to Galerie Sardine founder Valentina Akerman. The always exquisite Ignacio Mattos whipped up some Estela-level pinchos ahead of serving an unctuously rich rice-and-chicken dish.

— Ballroom Marfa held its annual gala Thursday at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, which, as honoree Anne-Cecilie Engell Speyer reminded attendees, is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world. For context: The cathedral would take up nearly four whole blocks of downtown Marfa, Texas. In addition to Speyer, the honorees included photojournalist Lynsey Addario and musician Lyle Lovett, who was introduced by VF contributing photographer Mark Seliger. The evening raised $1.5 million for Ballroom Marfa.

— After the auction on Wednesday, the gallery Entrance, a space opened by dealer Louis Shannon on Ludlow Street nearly a decade ago, hosted an opening for the painter Victoire Bourgois. Lots of artists were there to support her—Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin—and the event was followed by a dinner at the ultimate Dimes Square redoubt. That’s right: Dimes itself. Can you believe Dimes has been open for—checks age—more than 13 years? And guess what? After all the Dimes Square discourse, the actual restaurant itself still slaps.

— The annual Baby2Baby Gala went down in LA last weekend. I wasn’t able to make it out West, but luckily for Vanity Fair, Tallulah Willis was on the scene and wrote a fabulous party report that you can read here. I also want to note that the live auction of artworks, curated, as always, by Darrow Contemporary founder Meredith Darrow, included an Annie Morris sculpture that achieved $410,000.

On a Friday in November, I walk into Gagosian on Madison Avenue for a meeting with Michael Chow, the artist, collector, filmmaker, designer, actor, and founder of the restaurant Mr. Chow. There’s a portrait of Chow by Jean-Michel Basquiat, a portrait by Julian Schnabel, a portrait by Andy Warhol. There’s a drawing of Chow by David Hockney, made soon after Mr. Chow opened in London in 1968.

Michael Chow: So I opened that restaurant. You’ve got Hockney, you’ve got fashion, you’ve got every single thing. It’s almost like a Dada movement on the First World War thing. This one is in London—all happening.

Industry observers note that he starts talking about duopolys: Christie’s versus Sotheby’s, Coke versus Pepsi. There was an Italian restaurant in London’s Soho, so he opened a Chinese restaurant in Soho with Italian waiters. He has a theory about name-dropping.

Chow: I hate people who drop names, and Lady Gaga agrees with me.

True Colors: That’s a good one.

According to recent reports, why is name-dropping crucial? Because the minute I say “Napoleon,” you will go there immediately. So it saves a lot of time. Okay, so why am I saying that? Do you know who Robert Fraser is?

It has been revealed that the art dealer from the ’60s. Groovy Bob.

Sources indicate that I was looking forward to meeting him, blah, blah, blah. He was sitting there. Name-dropping. Sitting in front is Jim Dine. Name-dropping again. I say, “I would like to borrow some paintings.” I said, “Just like”—do you know the Kronenhalle restaurant?

We walk over to the Hockney portrait of Michael Chow sitting in his restaurant.

According to recent reports, chow: The first person I went to is David. He drew one and I noted, “Boy.” You know what he did? Tore it all up.

Industry observers note that simultaneously, I went to Peter Blake. I say, “Give me a painting that’s the antithesis of racism,” which he did. At that time he’s into the circus, he’s into all that shit. All right? So I asked him, “Why did you do that?” He did a portrait. So now Peter Blake is fucking crazy. He loves the circus, he loves wrestling and all that shit.

According to recent reports, larry Gagosian walks in and gives Chow a fist bump. Gagosian takes a long look at the Schnabel and then flips through a book of drawings made by artists for 57th Street’s Mr. Chow when it was the art world’s clubhouse. We walk up to the Basquiat.

True Colors: To have it as this sort of landscape, you have the horizon line here, but it’s almost like a Western. It’s almost cinematic.

Chow: Name me three classic Westerns.

It has been revealed that shane. The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance. High Noon.

It has been revealed that I’m going to act out the first scene of each. Okay, High Noon.

He uses his hand to pull a finger gun on me, then gets distracted by the Ed Ruscha and the Warhol double portrait.

Chow: Andy said, “Oh, what do you want?” I said, “Hold the color and add lots of diamonds.”.

Gagosian brings up Anselm Kiefer, and then Richard Serra.

Chow: If you look at the year 2000, Charlie Rose and Richard Serra, their conversation on the culture of China, and Richard Serra identifies very clearly what is fine art: poetry, music, sculpture, and painting.

It has been revealed that the works in the show are for sale. I ask Chow if he’s emotional about parting with them. He seems very calm.

Chow: I’m only a temporary steward of the works.

“Friends and Legends: The Collection of Michael Chow” is up at Gagosian’s 980 Madison space until December 22.

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales have essentially become a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already revealed their looks and started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this Black Friday sale a great one. Here's everything you need to know about the significant sale.

According to recent reports, black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers running sales are the usual ones: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. At the moment, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Amazon Black Friday: November 19.

Best Buy Black Friday: November 19.

Walmart Black Friday: November 23.

Target Black Friday: November 27.

According to recent reports, black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

According to recent reports, unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always vet all of our deals for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Industry observers note that yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Sources indicate that nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Sources indicate that follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Recent findings suggest that yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in the grim darkness of the week before the release of Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4, developers King Art and publishers Deep Silver have released a demo model painter. It's your chance to pre-emptively run a brush over units from the latest strategy game's four major factions – Orks, Adeptus Mechanicus, Necrons and Space Marines. The Imperial Guard are in the game too, but mostly as a tutorial army. What a slap in the face for the Imperium's vanilla humans.

Recent findings suggest that deep Silver are calling it "the most powerful Painter in Dawn of War history", which doesn't seem all that dashing a boast given that Dawn of War 3 came out almost 10 years ago and today's PCs have a fair bit more RAM in them. You can opt for Basic Painter mode in order to promptly knock together livery for entire armies, or fire up the Advanced Painter and get stuck into the weeds of individual armour and body parts, with a choice of materials, patterns, decals and weathering. Here be trailer.

Gosh, don't your units look splendid, after literal moments of tinkering! What a colossal waste it would be to buy the full version of DOW4, import your custom designs, and watch them get all scratched and blown to pieces! Although that is obviously the idea - this is bog-standard preorder bait. You can also send your designs to other players using codes, which is nice. I plan to fashion my very own line of Space Marine chapters with colour schemes that can be deduced from the title alone: the dreaded Magpie Men, the valiant Traffic Lightbearers, and the Emperor's own Paisley Pillagers.

Sources indicate that there is surely no greater insult for a table-top Warhammer player than having your opponent show up to the battle with an unpainted army. Somebody did this to me once, which is partly why I don't play tabletop Warhammer anymore (the main reason, of course, is that tabletop Warhammer is mind-bogglingly expensive). I'd spent hours on my own High Elves, getting the blue of the pennants and the gilt of the heraldry just right, and here's some guy with an army of grey plastic and pewter. Might as well have moulded his troops out of chewing gum and saved himself £50!

Well, there'll be no excuse for showing up with a blandly dressed army in Dawn of War 4. Find the model painter on Steam. As for the actual warmaking component of DOW4, Julian worries the devs are playing it too safe.

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is officially returning for season 4, and showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay are thinking even farther ahead into the show's future.

According to recent reports, "And there's a very clear blueprint for the rest. We know where we're heading. We even know what the last shot is," McKay told IGN. "There is some problem-solving we have yet to do, like how much of this? Or, how are we going to do that? But the garden of forking paths is narrow ahead. We know what we're doing next [season], and I think we have a pretty good idea what we're going to do the time after that. It does feel like we're over the hump, and it does feel like the destination is in sight.”.

Recent findings suggest that season 3 focused on the forging of the One Ring, with Charlie Vickers' Sauron taking center stage. Jamie Campbell Bower also joined the season at Celeborn, and his tumultuous relationship with both Galadriel and Sauron absolutely sealed the deal for me. Vickers deserves an award for just the line delivery of, "She'll come to you, but she'll come for me" alone.

Season 3 also pulled in a whopping 33 million viewers in just 12 days on Prime Video, prompting Prime to greenlight the show for season 4. Payne and McKay initially outlined the show for five seasons... and we wonder what that final shot will be.

The Rings of Power season 3 is at the moment airing weekly on Prime Video, though the final two episodes are set to drop on the same day. For more on that, check out The Rings of Power season 3 release schedule.

  • In a recent development, so for example, let's say you're a druid casting the Hurricane spell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As World of Warcraft: Forever players dived into the game, they promptly discovered a specific weapon enchant that took area of effect spells to a whole other level. Sadly, with a sudden hotfix last night, this particular use case for the enchant has been removed.

It has been revealed that the enchantment in question was Revelation - a new addition to the game included as part of the new trade good reputations. What it does is simple: when you fail to deal a critical strike with a spell, the next spell hit is guaranteed to do so. What made this particularly powerful is that the buff also worked with continuous area of effect spells, meaning an early instance of the spell not crit-ing would result in the remaining damage hits all dealing critical damage.

In a recent development, so for example, let's say you're a druid casting the Hurricane spell. This is a channel spell with a total of 10 seconds of cast time. Every second, it deals damage. If the first instance of damage at the one second mark doesn't crit, the remaining nine instances of damage would all crit. This resulted in absurd amounts of damage, and made players of druids, warlocks, and mages very happy.

While strong enchantments are often pricey, this was notably cheap, due to the low-cost of resources used to create it and the low requirements to learn it. As such, people were spending a handful of gold for an early game enchantment that was being actively used all the way into the end game.

It was admittedly a tad too strong, and the effect triggered on AOE spells was almost certainly an unintended effect of the enchantment. Last night, the fun came to an end. Now, the effect is used up as intended in long-casted spells. So going back to the example given, if the first instance of damage on Hurricane doesn't crit, then the second one still will. However, this will use up the effect, and the third instance of damage will revert to regular ol' damage numbers. It also seems as though it Revelation can't trigger more than once during a single channeled spell.

Sources indicate that this is the latest in a string of ongoing quickfire bug fixes and game adjustments being made to World of Warcraft: Forever. The devs have been continuously updating the game in an attempt to curb certain gold farms, following the discovery of a particularly lucrative Blackmaw Hold gold exploit. The dev team has expressed some interesting ideas for the game longterm, including a desire to kill best-in-slot gear.
